content: 1. Systematic reviews have reported mixed findings, with some studies demonstrating benefits of interventions while others showed no significant effects. 2. Most of the studies were conducted in high-income countries, primarily in the USA and the UK. 3. In the absence of a meta-analysis, it is challenging to comprehensively assess the overall impact of these interventions. 4. Three studies provided low-quality evidence suggesting that interprofessional education may lead to changes in the use of clinical guidelines or standards. 5. The authors of the systematic reviews did not report a pooled effect estimate. 6. Transforming and scaling up health professionals’ education and training is a critical area of focus. 7. Accreditation by national governments in the education of health professionals has been shown to positively influence individuals seeking membership in professional organizations, though the evidence quality is low. 8. Continuous professional development (CPD) programs have been associated with improved observed and self-reported clinical practices, as evidenced by randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and consistent findings from non-randomized studies. 9. Faculty development programs that update and enhance teaching and clinical skills in undergraduate and postgraduate settings are recommended, particularly when linked to promotion and reward systems. 10. Effective teaching has the potential to influence trainee performance, which may ultimately impact patient and population health outcomes. 11. The absence of higher education policies mandating faculty development in health professionals’ education is a significant barrier. 12. Innovative approaches, such as recruiting community-based clinicians and health workers as educators, are necessary to address the shortage of faculty and scale up health professionals’ training. 13. The recruitment of community-based educators can increase the number of available trainers, enabling the training of more health professionals, though care must be taken to maintain training standards. 14. Embedding faculty development in accreditation processes and establishing dedicated teaching teams are strategies to enhance teaching quality and capacity. 15. Resistance from traditional health professional schools, often rooted in hierarchical structures based on scientific achievement and research, may pose challenges to implementing innovative faculty expansion strategies. 16. Dual appointments of educators in schools and health facilities, as well as adjunct appointments of clinicians as educators, have been successful in rapidly scaling up faculty in various settings. 17. High-quality research is needed to evaluate the impact of faculty development initiatives on patient outcomes, population health, and the effectiveness of teaching rewards on faculty development. 18. The anticipated benefits of innovative faculty expansion, such as increased training capacity for health professionals, are likely to outweigh the associated costs, provided there is appropriate selection and support for educators. 19. Faculty development programs should incorporate principles of adult learning, offer diverse educational methods, and be evaluated rigorously to demonstrate their effectiveness. 20. Addressing the misalignment of faculty with service delivery needs requires the implementation of higher education policies that mandate faculty development programs linked to funding, promotion, and reward systems. 21. The recruitment of community-based educators, particularly in underserved areas, is seen as a realistic option to address faculty shortages and improve health equity. 22. Faculty development initiatives must be context-specific and tailored to the needs of the population and the health system. 23. The balance of desirable and undesirable consequences of faculty development programs varies across settings, but the overall benefits are likely to outweigh the costs in most cases. 24. Governments, funders, and accrediting bodies should prioritize the implementation of mandatory faculty development programs to enhance the quality, quantity, and relevance of health professionals’ education. 25. Monitoring and evaluation of faculty development initiatives are essential to ensure their effectiveness and alignment with health system goals.
